passages.text: Physical Examination Findings r Early—from 30 minutes to 12 hours post-ingestion in dogs; nausea and vomiting; mild to severe depression; ataxia and knuckling; muscle fasciculations; nystagmus; head tremors; decreased withdrawal reflexes and righting ability; polyuria and polydipsia. r Dogs—with increasing depression, patient drinks less but polyuria continues, resulting in dehydration; CNS signs abate transiently after approximately 12 hours, but recur later. r Cats—usually remain markedly depressed; do not exhibit polydipsia. r Oliguria (dogs, 36–72 hours; cats, 12–24 hours) and anuria (72–96 hours post-ingestion)—often develop if untreated. r May note severe hypothermia. r Severe lethargy or coma. r Seizures. r Anorexia. r Vomiting. r Oral ulcers. r Salivation. r Kidneys—often swollen and painful, particularly in cats. CAUSES Ingestion of ethylene glycol, the principal component (95%) of most antifreeze solutions. RISK FACTORS Access to ethylene glycol—widespread availability; somewhat pleasant taste; small minimum lethal dose; lack of public awareness of toxicity. DIAGNOSIS DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS r Acute (30 minutes–12 hours post-ingestion)—ethanol, methanol, and marijuana toxicosis; ketoacidotic diabetes mellitus; pancreatitis; gastroenteritis. r Renal stage—acute renal failure by nephrotoxins (e.g., aminoglycoside antibiotics, amphotericin B, cancer chemotherapeutic drugs, ibuprofen, oxalate-containing plants such as philodendrons, plants of the lily family [cats], cyclosporin, grape and raisin toxicosis [causes hypercalcemia, unlike ethylene glycol toxicosis], and heavy metals); leptospirosis, tubulointerstitial nephritis; glomerular and vascular disease; renal ischemia (hypoperfusion). CBC/BIOCHEMISTRY/URINALYSIS r PCV and total protein—often high owing to dehydration. r Stress leukogram— common. r High BUN and creatinine—dog, 36–48 hours post-ingestion; cat, 12 hours post-ingestion. r Hyperphosphatemia may occur transiently 3–6 hours post-ingestion, owing to phosphate rust inhibitors in the antifreeze; hyperphosphatemia is also seen with azotemia owing to decreased glomerular filtration. r Hyperkalemia if oliguric or anuric. r Hypocalcemia—occurs in approximately half of patients, owing to chelation of calcium by oxalic acid; clinical signs infrequently observed because of acidosis. r Hyperglycemia—occurs in approximately half of patients, owing to inhibition of glucose metabolism by aldehydes, increased epinephrine and endogenous corticosteroids, and uremia.

passages.text: r EG serum concentration— peaks 1–6 hours post-ingestion; usually not detectable in the serum or urine by 72 hours. r Commercial kits: PRN Pharmacol REACT EG measures concentrations at > 50 mg/dL; estimate by multiplying the osmole gap by 6.2. ◦Test does not detect metabolites so must be used within the first few hours post-ingestion. ◦Results are available in 6 minutes but should not be read over 10 minutes. ◦Labeled for dogs and cats. Some cats may have toxicosis at levels below 50 mg/dL. ◦False-positive test results can be seen with propylene glycol, glycerol, mannitol, and sorbitol. Ethanol may combine with propylene glycol or glycerol to give a false positive. r Woods lamp examination of urine, face, paws, or vomitus may detect fluorescein that is sometimes added to antifreeze. This method is non-specific and may be unreliable. IMAGING Ultrasonography—renal cortices may be hyperechoic as a result of crystals. DIAGNOSTIC PROCEDURES r Kidney biopsy—with anuria; confirm diagnosis. r Cytologic examination of kidney imprints—often diagnostic; numerous calcium oxalate crystals. (Continued) Ethylene Glycol Toxicosis E PATHOLOGIC FINDINGS r Kidneys often swollen. r Post-mortem examination of kidney reveals the presence of calcium oxalate crystals in the tubules. TREATMENT APPROPRIATE HEALTH CARE r Cats—usually inpatient. r Dogs—usually outpatient if < 5 hours post-ingestion and treated with fomepizole; inpatient if > 5 hours for intravenous fluids to correct dehydration, increase tissue perfusion, and promote diuresis. NURSING CARE r Goals—prevent absorption; increase excretion; prevent metabolism. r Induction of vomiting and gastric lavage with activated charcoal not recommended unless can be performed in first 30 minutes following ingestion due to the rapid absorption of ethylene glycol. r Intravenous fluids—correct dehydration, increase tissue perfusion, and promote diuresis; accompanied by bicarbonate given slowly intravenously to correct metabolic acidosis. r Monitor serial plasma bicarbonate concentrations—0.5 × body weight (kg) × (24 – plasma bicarbonate) = sodium bicarbonate needed (mEq). r Monitor urine pH in response to therapy. r Azotemia and oliguric renal failure (dogs)—most of the ethylene glycol has been metabolized; little benefit from inhibition of ADH; correct fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base disorders; establish diuresis; diuretics (particularly mannitol) may help; hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis may be useful; may need extended treatment (several weeks) before renal function is re-established.

passages.text: Pigs and cattle often develop renal and pe1irenal edema. Pigs may also have pulmonary edema witl1 tan fluid in the pleural and peritoneal cavities. Poultry usually do not develop gross lesions. Diagnosis: Diagnosis is often difficult because the nonspecific multisystemic signs may appear similai· to other types of CNS disease or traunm, gastroente1itis, pancreatitis, ketoacidotic diabetes mellitus, and acute renal failw·e due to renal ischemia or other nephrotoxicants. If ingestion of EG is not witnessed, diagnosis is usually based on a combination of history, physical examination, and laboratory data. ETHYLENE GLYCOL TOXICITY Within 3 hr of ingestion of toxic doses ofEG, dogs and cats develop normochlo­ remic metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap, minimally concentrated or isosthenwic urine with an acidic pH, and marked serU111 hyperosmolality with an increased osmolal gap. Sel'U111 osmolality can be increased as much as 100 mOsm/kg above normal (280--310 mOsm/kg) within 3 hr ofEG ingestion. TI1e difference between measured and calculated (1.86 [Na•+ K•] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 + 9) osmolality is referred to as the osmolal gap. The gap is caused by the presence of osmotically active particles ( eg, ethylene glycol) in the sel'U111 that are not factored into the above equation. Calcium oxalate crystalhnia may be observed as early as 3 and 6 hr after ingestion in cats and dogs, respectively. Monohydrate calciU111 oxalate crystals ( clear, 6--sided prisms) are more com­ mon than dihydrate calciU111 oxalate crystals (maltese cross or envelope-shaped). EG concentrations in sel'Uln and urine are detect­ able by 1-2 hr after ingestion. Conunercial test kits can detect sefU111 EG concentrations of Ē50 mg/clL. Some antifreeze preparations contain fluorescein, which appears b1ight yellow-green when viewed U11der a Wood's lamp. Urine fluorescence has been used as a qualitative adjU11ctive test in suspected EG ingestions in people and may be of value in veterinaiy medicine. Hyperphosphaternia has been seen in dogs within 3 hr of ingestion of commercial antifreeze solutions that contain phosphate rust inhibitors. This hype1phosphatemia resolves before the onset of EG-induced acute renal failure and azotemia, then recurs when the animal becomes azotemic. Treatment: The prognosis vai·ies inversely with the ainoU11t of tinle that elapses-between ingestion and initiation of treatment.

Calciwn oxalate crystalluria occurs less commonly in dogs and cats. If persistent, it may indicate an increased risk of calciwn oxalate urolith fotmation, which has been increasing in some countries throughout the past few yeai·s. (See also UROLITI-IIASIS, p 1502, and p 1525.) However, calciwn oxalate and calciw11 carbonate crystallwia is common in healthy horses and cattle. Calciw11 oxalate diliydrate crystals appear as squares with an "X" in the middle, or "envelope­ shaped." Calcium oxalate monohydrate c1ystals are "dwnb-bell" shaped. An unusual fonn of calciwn oxalate crystals is typically seen in association with ethylene glycol toxicity (seep 3046). These crystals are found in neutral to acidic urine. They ai·e small, flat, and colorless and ai·e shaped like "picket fence posts." Ammoniwn acid urate crystals suggest liver disease ( eg, portosystemic shunt). These crystals occur in acidic urine and ai·e yellow-brown spheres with irregular, spiny projections; however, they may also be atnorphous. Certain species, such as birds and reptiles, and certain breeds of dogs, specifically Dalmatians, can nom1ally have atrunoniun1 acid urate crystalluria Cystine crystals are six-sided and of variable size. They are seen in acidic urine. Presence of cystine crystals represents a proximal tubular defect in amino acid reabsorption. Cystinuria has been reported in many breeds of dogs and rarely in cats. Dachshunds, Newfoundlands, English Bulldogs, and Scottish Terriers have a high incidence of cystine urolithiasis. Bilirubin crystals occur with bilirubinu­ ria; however, they may be normal in small numbers in dogs. Lipids: Fat droplets are commonly present in urine from dogs and cats and may be mistaken for RBCs. They often vary in size and tend to float on a different plane of focus than the remainder of the sediment. They are not considered to be pathologic. Spermatozoa: Spermatozoa may be seen norn1ally in urine collected from reproduc­ tively intact male dogs. Plant Material: Occasionally, plant material may be seen in urine samples collected by voiding. When present, they indicate contamination of the urine san1ple and are not pathologic. Bladder Tumor Antigen Test The bladder tumor antigen test can be used to screen for transitional cell carcinoma in dogs. The results are not specific for transitional cell carcinoma, and non-neo­ plastic disease ( eg, urinary tract infections, hematuria, etc) can give positive results.

Clinicopathologic findings can include azotemia, hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, increased alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity, hyperglycemia, hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, isosthenuria, hyposthenuria, proteinuria, glucosuria, pyuria, crystalluria, and cylindruria.40 If no contraindications to emesis exist, exposed patients should have emesis induced (ch. 132). Induction of emesis can be rewarding even up to 12 hours post-exposure. AC should be given only to patients with large exposures and poor emesis results. Patients should have a baseline renal chemistry profile and urinalysis. If decontamination is highly successful and the risk of AKI is considered low, then patients can be monitored at home. Since spontaneous vomiting is often the earliest indicator of AKI, if possible, these patients should not be given an antiemetic prior to discharge so as not to mask the development of any vomiting. Patients should have a renal chemistry profile and urinalysis rechecked at 24-48 hours post exposure or sooner if any clinical signs develop at home. If decontamination is incompletely successful, then the patient should be admitted to the hospital for isotonic crystalloid fluid diuresis for 48 hours. Renal profiles and urinalyses should still be monitored. Most patients that are promptly treated with fluid diuresis do not develop AKI. Since the tubular basement membrane remains intact and epithelial regeneration has been seen histopathologically, recovery is possible if the condition is managed proactively. Clinical signs of ataxia, oliguria, and/or weakness; an elevated Ca × P product; and hyperkalemia have been correlated with a poorer prognosis.40 References 1. Gwaltney-Brant S.M. Renal toxicology. Small Animal Toxicology. 3rd ed. Elsevier; 2013:489–498. 3. Parker V.J, Rudinsky A.J, Chew D.J. Vitamin D metabolism in canine and feline medicine. J Am Vet Med Assoc. 2017;250:1259–1269. 4. passages.text: Then, 12-24 hours after ingestion, cardiopulmonary involvement inconsistently develops (e.g., heart failure). Third, 1 to 3 days later, animals commonly develop oliguric AKI, renomegaly, and signs that include obtundation, anorexia, vomiting, evidence of renal pain, hypothermia, coma, and ultimately death. Unfortunately, many animals are not seen before the third phase. Initial laboratory results may show hypocalcemia and increased anion gap metabolic acidosis. Some blood gas machines falsely record glycol as lactate, yielding spurious severe hyperlactatemia.52,53 Ultrasound (US) shows enlarged and markedly hyperechoic kidneys ( Video 300.1). Initial treatment should be aimed at prevention of gastrointestinal (GI) absorption. Emesis should be induced and activated charcoal administered to animals in phase 1 (ch. 132). Hemodialysis can remove nearly all absorbed ethylene glycol from the bloodstream.54 IV fluids may be helpful in maintaining renal tubular flow (ch. 120). If discovered in the early stages, 4-methylpyrazole (4-MP, fomepizole) can prevent metabolism of ethylene glycol by effectively inactivating alcohol dehydrogenase in dogs, preventing formation of oxalic acid and its renal toxicity. It does not cause the side effects of ethanol and is the treatment of choice.55-57 Alternatively, IV ethanol is given to competitively inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase. 4-MP and ethanol are of little benefit once renal damage has occurred. The prognosis at this stage is guarded to poor.58-60 Melamine Intoxication (ch. 135) In March of 2007 several brands of pet food were recalled in the United States due to melamine contamination. Affected animals developed anorexia, vomiting, lethargy, PU/PD and AKI.61 Toxicology studies identified 2 contaminants: melamine and cyanuric acid. When these compounds are co-ingested, they form an insoluble precipitate in kidney tubules that causes renal failure via physical blockage, as confirmed in studies on rats.62 Melamine, a compound used in fertilizer and soft plastics, was probably added to the dog food to increase the reported protein content.63 Histopathologic examination of affected kidneys revealed intratubular crystalluria, tubular necrosis with regeneration, and subcapsular perivascular inflammation.64 Many affected animals either died or were euthanized. Those that survived did eventually have recovery or improvement in renal function. More recently (2007-present) dogs that had received jerky or sweet potato treats manufactured in China have developed various acquired renal dysfunctions. These maladies include oligoanuric AKI, Fanconi syndrome, and other tubular defects (ch. 303). Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D) Intoxication (ch.

passages.text: To try to identify individuals sensitive to high-dose ivermectin, an increasing dosage schedule has been proposed.* For the first 5 days of treatment, the dog is given 50, 100, 150, 200 and 300 yg/kg of ivermectin, respectively. If the dog is highly sensitive to high-dose ivermectin, subtle neurologic signs, for example, lethargy, ataxia, should develop within 24 hours of the administration of the sensitizing dosage. If the drug is discontinued immediately, the dog should return to normal within 24 to 48 hours. Because some dogs do not develop these signs for weeks, the owner should always observe the dog carefully. Collies sensitive to high-dose ivermectin also are sensitive to high-dose milbemycin when the dosage exceeds 5 mg/kg.** Cross sensitivity to doramectin and moxidectin remains untested but should be expected. High-dose milbemycin has been used to treat hundreds of dogs with demodicosis and scabies, and neurologic side effects have not been reported, even in ivermectin-sensitive breeds, with dosages below 3 mg/kg. In a recent study of 70 dogs with nasal mite infestation, milbemycin was given weekly for three consecutive weeks at dosages of 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg. Sixteen dogs had side effects. In 12, one or more episodes of vomiting or diarrhea, or both, occurred. Two dogs seemed lethargic, one was uncoordinated, and the last dog’s sneezing worsened with treatment. The dosage used did not seem to influence the frequency of side effects, and a breed frequency was not reported. All dogs return to normal within 48 hours of drug withdrawal. When moxidectin was given to ivermectin-sensitive collies, no toxicity was seen with 15 yg/kg monthly.!* However, when it was given at 90 g/kg, mild signs of toxicity were seen. Ivermectin Ivermectin (Ivomec, Merial) is a derivative of avermectin B from fermentation products of Streptomyces avermitilis. This drug is noted for activity against nematodes, microfilaria, and Sarcoptes, Cheyletiella, Notoedres, and Otodectes mites. Although ivermectin was not shown to be efficacious for Demodex with the treatment protocols that had been effective for other ectoparasites (e.g., 0.2 to 0.4 mg/kg, orally or subcutaneously, weekly for up to 8 weeks), it can be effective when it is administered orally daily. Ivermectin does not affect trematodes and cestodes, because GABA is not involved in neurotransmission in those species.

passages.text: In cattle, toxic effects generally do not appear until dosages of 30x those recommended are injected. At 8 mg/kg, cattle showed signs of ataxia, listlessness, and occasionally, death. Sheep have shown signs of ataxia and depression at ivermectin doses of 4 mg/kg. Swine have shown signs of toxicosis (lethargy, ataxia, tremors, lateral recumbency, and mydriasis) at doses of 30 mg/kg. Neonatal pigs may be more susceptible to ivermectin overdosages, presumably due to a more permeable blood-brain barrier. Accurate dosing practices are recommended. Drug Interactions The following drug interactions have either been reported or are theoretical in humans or animals receiving ivermectin and may be of significance in veterinary patients: BENZODIAZEPINES: Effects may be potentiated by ivermectin; use together not advised in humans KETAMINE: It has been recommended not to use ivermectin in reptiles within 10 days of ketamine (Bays 2009) SPINOSAD (Comfortis®): It has been recommended not to use with the high extra-label doses of ivermectin (Kuhl 2009) Caution is advised if using other drugs that can inhibit p-glycoprotein. Those dogs at risk for ABCB1-1∆ (formerly MDR1 allele) mutation (Collies, Australian Shepherds, Shelties, Long-haired Whippet, etc., “white feet”) should probably not receive ivermectin with the following drugs, unless tested “normal”; at least one reference states that ivermectin should never be used with ketoconazole in dogs (Waisglass 2009). Drugs and drug classes involved include: AMIODARONE CARVEDILOL CLARITHROMYCIN CYCLOSPORINE DILTIAZEM ERYTHROMYCIN ITRACONAZOLE KETOCONAZOLE QUINIDINE SPIRONOLACTONE TAMOXIFEN VERAPAMIL Laboratory Considerations When used at microfilaricide dosages, ivermectin may yield false-negative results in animals with occult heartworm infection. Doses DOGS: Note: When used for prophylaxis or treatment of dirofilariasis it is suggested to review the guidelines published by the American Heartworm Society at www.heartwormsociety.org for more information. As a preventative for heartworm: a) 6–12 micrograms/kg PO once monthly (Knight 2000) b) Minimum dosage of 6 micrograms/kg (0.006 mg/kg) PO per month. (Package insert; Heartgard30®—Merial) As a microfilaricide: a) When used to kill third, fourth, and young fifth stage larvae for prophylaxis or to kill these larval stages prior to adulticide therapy along with microfilariae, ivermectin is dosed at 6–12 micro-grams/kg PO once a month.

■Ivermectin: r Off-label use for demodicosis r Macrocyclic lactone with GABA agonist activity r Binds to chloride channels in the mite’s nervous system, causing paralysis and death r Safety in mammals is due to the lack of glutamate-gated chloride channels in the peripheral nervous system and the restriction of GABA-gated channels in the central nervous system (which is protected by the blood–brain barrier) r Contraindicated in collies, Shetland sheepdogs, Australian shepherds, Old English sheepdogs, white German shepherds, long-haired whippets, greyhounds, silken windhound, other herding breeds, and crosses with these breeds r Ivermectin sensitivity: derived from a deletion mutation of the multidrugresistant gene (ABCB1) resulting in a truncated nonfunctional protein called P-glycoprotein; P-glycoprotein is a transmembrane protein transporter found in the blood–brain barrier; P-glycoprotein pumps ivermectin within the brain back into the blood; testing for this mutation is available through the Washington State University Veterinary Clinical Pharmacology Laboratory (www.vetmed.wsu.edu.vcpl) r Toxicity seen as hypersalivation, mydriasis, tremors, depression, ataxia, blindness r Intravenous lipid emulsion therapy has shown success in the treatment of ivermectin toxicosis r Do not use with Spinosad-containing flea control products; enhances toxicity of ivermectin r Demodex otitis can be treated with 0.01% ivermectin solution r Oral administration of the injectable formulation: 0.3–0.6 mg/kg q24h r Administer 120 μg/kg q24h for the first 3 days to identify ivermectin-sensitive breeds (ABCB1 mutation): alternative dosing – gradual dose increase from 0.05 mg/kg on day 1; 0.1 mg/kg on day 2; 0.15 mg/kg on day 3; 0.2 mg/kg on day 4; 0.3 mg/kg on day 5: continued increases of 0.1 mg/kg daily if necessary to administer maximum dosage of 0.6 mg/kg q24h r Treat for 60 days beyond negative skin scrapings (average 3–8 months) r Continue rinses for at least 1 month following negative skin scrapings. ■Milbemycin: r Off-label use for demodicosis r Macrocyclic lactone with GABA agonist activity r Dosage of 1 mg/kg PO q24h cures 50% of cases; 2 mg/kg PO q24h cures 85% of cases; oral dose recommendations range between 1.5 and 3.1 mg/kg/day r Treat for 60 days beyond multiple negative skin scrapings r Ivermectin-sensitive breeds (ABCB1 defect) generally tolerate milbemycin r Side effects are similar to ivermectin (depression, stupor, coma, ataxia, seizures) r Major limitation of the drug is expense r Demodex otitis can be treated with 0.1% milbemycin oxime topical.

passages.text: In general, these drugs are effective for nematodes, microfilaria, lice, fur mites, Otodectes, Sarcoptes, Notoedres, Cheyletiella, and Demodex. Ivermectin, milbemycin, and moxidectin are licensed for use orally every 30 days at 0.625 pg/kg, 0.5 mg/kg, and 3 pg/kg, respectively, for the prevention of dirofilariasis. At this dosage, no adverse side effects are seen in dogs of any breeding. In treating external parasites, ivermectin is administered at 200 to 600 g/kg daily, weekly, or bimonthly and toxic side effects can be seen. Milbemycin is administered at 1 to 2 mg/kg daily or weekly, and toxic side effects, although rare, have been reported. Selamectin is a novel new avermectin that has been shown to be efficacious for the treatment of fleas,3!4 ear mites, scabies, ticks, some intestinal nematodes, and prevention of heartworms. It is applied topically and absorbed systemically, with efficacy for fleas and heartworms shown with once-monthly dosing for both dogs and cats. High-dose ivermectin or milbemycin can be toxic to dogs younger than 3 months of age and to adult dogs within certain breeds. Breeds widely reported to be sensitive to high-dose ivermectin include the collie, Old English sheep dog, Australian shepherd, Shetland sheepdog, and crosses thereof.24* Individual reports of an adverse reaction in a border collie, West Highland White terrier, German shepherd dog, and Samoyed can be found.** Toxic side effects are neurologic in origin and include mydriasis, hypersalivation, lethargy, ataxia, tremors, coma, and death. Ivermectin-sensitive collies lack adequate quantities of P-glycoprotein necessary to successfully exclude ivermectin from the brain.!°* In breeds very sensitive to high-dose ivermectin, for example, the collie, one dose of more than 125 yg/kg can produce coma. In less sensitive individuals, side effects may not be seen for days to weeks. To try to identify individuals sensitive to high-dose ivermectin, an increasing dosage schedule has been proposed.* For the first 5 days of treatment, the dog is given 50, 100, 150, 200 and 300 yg/kg of ivermectin, respectively. If the dog is highly sensitive to high-dose ivermectin, subtle neurologic signs, for example, lethargy, ataxia, should develop within 24 hours of the administration of the sensitizing dosage.

passages.text: Swine: Volume of distribution = 4 L/kg; elimination half-life = 0.5 days. Sheep: Bioavailability = 1 (intra-abomasal), 0.25 (intra-ruminal); volume of distribution = 4.6 L/kg; elimination half-life = 2–7 days. Contraindications/Precautions/Warnings The manufacturer recommends that ivermectin not be used in foals less than 4 months old, as safety of the drug in animals this young has not been firmly established. However, foals less than 30 days of age have tolerated doses as high as 1 mg/kg without signs of toxicity. Ivermectin is not recommended for use in puppies less than 6 weeks old. After receiving heartworm prophylaxis doses, the manufacturer recommends observing Collie-type breeds for at least 8 hours after administration. Most clinicians feel that ivermectin should not be used in breeds susceptible (Collies, Shelties, Australian shepherds, etc.) to the ABCB1-1∆ (formerly MDR1-allele) mutation at the doses specified for treating microfilaria or other parasites unless the patient has been tested and found not to have the gene defect. A specific test for identifying dogs that have the gene defect (deletion mutation of the ABCB1-1∆ (formerly MDR1 gene) is now available. Contact the veterinary clinical pharmacology lab at www.vetmed.wsu.edu. Ivermectin is reportedly contraindicated in chelonians, Indigo snakes and skinks. Milbemycin has reportedly been given safely to chelonians. Because milk withdrawal times have not been established, the drug is not FDA-approved for use in lactating dairy animals or females of breeding age. The injectable products for use in cattle and swine should be given subcutaneously only; do not give IM or IV. If using a product in a species not labeled for that product (extra-label), be certain of the dosage and/or dilutions. There are many reports of overdoses in small animals when large animal products have been used. Adverse Effects In horses, swelling and pruritus at the ventral mid-line can be seen approximately 24 hours after ivermectin administration due to a hypersensitivity reaction to dead Onchocerca spp. microfilaria. The reaction is preventable by administering a glucocorticoid just prior to, and for 1–2 days after ivermectin. If untreated, swelling usually subsides within 7–10 days and pruritus will resolve within 3 weeks. Dogs may exhibit a shock-like reaction when ivermectin is used as a microfilaricide, presumably due to a reaction associated with the dying microfilaria. Other adverse effects when used as a microfilaricide include depression, hypothermia, and vomiting.

Alternatively, treatment with ivermectin 0.20.6 mg/kg PO every 24 hours is often effective against generalized demodicosis. Initially, ivermectin 0.1 mg/kg PO is administered on day 1, then 0.2 mg/kg PO is administered on day 2, with oral daily increments of 0.1 mg/kg until 0.20.6 mg/kg/day is being administered, assuming that no signs of toxicity develop. The cure rate for 0.6 mg/kg/day ivermectin is 85% to 90%. 7. Another effective alternative therapy is milbemycin oxime, 0.5 to 2 mg/kg PO every 24 hours. The cure rate is 85% to 90%, with the prognosis for cure being better for juvenile-onset cases than for adult-onset cases. 8. Doramectin is also reported to be effective against canine demodicosis at a dose of 0.6 mg/kg SC once weekly. The cure rate is approximately 85%. Adverse effects are uncommon but include, as for ivermectin, dilated pupils, lethargy, blindness, and coma. 9. For dogs 520 kS- the use of 9% amitraz collars may be effective. The dog's neck is shaved to ensure that the collar is in close contact with the skin, and the col1ar is replaced every 2 weeks for the duration of treatment. In small dogs, use of 9% amitraz collars alone may be as effective as ivermectin (0.6 mg/kg/day PO). Also, the combined use of oral ivermectin and 9% amitraz collars may be more effective than either oral ivermectin or 9% amitraz collars alone. 10. Moxidectin 1 % injectable for cattle has been reported effective when administered at a dosage of 0.4 mg/kg PO every 24 to 72 hours. However, adverse effects are common. 11. Regardless of the miticidal treatment chosen, therapy is administered over the long term (weeks to months). Treatments should be continued for at least 1 month beyond the time when follow-up skin scrapings become negative for mites. 12. The prognosis is good to fair. Relapses may occur, requiring periodic or lifelong treatment in some dogs. The use of glucocorticosteroids in any dog that has been d iagnosed with demodicosis should be avoided. Because of its hereditary predisposition, neither female nor male dogs with juvenileonset generalized demodicosis should be bred. 0 canis is not considered contagious to cats or to humans. It is transmitted from bitch to newborn puppies during the first 2 to 3 days of nursing, and possibly between adult dogs that are close cohabitants.

Larson L.J, Schultz R.D. Do two current canine parvovirus type 2 and 2b vaccines provide protection against the new type 2c variant? Vet Ther. 2008;9:94– CLIENT INFORMATION Canine and Feline Parvovirus WHAT IS PARVOVIRUS? This is one of the most common and serious viruses that puppies and kittens can contract. Viruses are much smaller than bacteria and they cannot cause disease unless they infect a living and multiplying cell in dog or cat. Parvoviruses are particularly small and attack the rapidly dividing cells of the body, which include the cells that line the intestine, the bone marrow, and cells of the immune system. Infection of the fetus can also cause very serious birth defects or death. WHICH ANIMALS ARE AT RISK? The disease affects mostly puppies and kittens, especially under about 4 months of age. Female dogs and cats that have been vaccinated provide antibodies to their young through their milk; these antibodies are absorbed within the first day after birth. These antibodies protect puppies and kittens for the first few weeks of life but after that they are fully susceptible. The antibodies provided by the mother in her milk prevent vaccinations from being effective. There is a window during which time the antibodies a puppy or kitten absorb from their mother are no longer sufficient to protect it from infection but are sufficient to prevent a vaccine from being effective. This is known as “the window of vulnerability” and is the reason why vaccination programs comprise 3 injections about a month apart starting at 4-6 weeks of age. The very last vaccine given (usually at 14-18 weeks of age) is the one that is most likely to be protective as there will be no antibodies from the mother left in the puppy or kitten’s system to destroy the vaccine by this point. The most common reason for vaccine failure is only partial completion of the vaccination series. Puppies and kittens catch the disease from other infected animals, from people who have had contact with infected animals, or from an environment that has been contaminated by infected animals. Parvovirus is very hardy and can survive for many months in soil and on surfaces. Household bleach diluted 1:30 and left on a surface for 30 minutes is an effective decontaminating agent. Steam cleaning is also effective. Hygiene and limiting contact with other animals until after the vaccination program is complete is strongly recommended. About 10 days after the last vaccination, a puppy or kitten will be immune. HOW WOULD I KNOW MY PUPPY OR KITTEN HAS PARVOVIRUS INFECTION? The first sign is usually lethargy and a loss of appetite.

passages.text: Immunosuppressed, parasitized, stressed, or malnourished animals and those incubating disease are not able to mount an adequate immune response to prevent disease. Clients should always be advised that such problems can occur. In most cases, an adequate immune response is not achieved before 10 to 14 days. An 8-week-old puppy may not develop a strong immune response to protect against an infectious disease if challenged by maternal antibodies because it is not feasible to check immune titers to determine the presence of maternal antibodies. So, in order for young animals to be protected and mount an immune response, they must receive vaccinations/ boosters at certain intervals. The most important dose is administered at 16 weeks of age or older, when almost all puppies should have lost MDA and are able to respond to the vaccine.4,11,12 Even with the administration of the last dose of vaccine at 16 weeks of age a small percentage of dogs may not respond adequately.3,4,8 High-titer MLV CPV-2 (either alone or combined with CDV) vaccines may be given from 4 weeks of age and have been used as a strategy to reduce the window of susceptibility.11,13 Moreover, a CDV canarypox vector recombinant vaccine, that can overcome the interference of maternal antibodies in puppies and appears to immunize puppies about 2-4 weeks earlier than MLV vaccines, is available in some countries.4,8 Since there are no guarantees that every puppy will have a rapid active immune response to these vaccines, puppies should be vaccinated every 2 to 4 weeks with CDV, CAV-2, and CPV-2 vaccines, up to 16 weeks of age.3,4,8 After an initial series of core vaccinations, it has been recommended to administer another set of core vaccines at 12 months of age. The purpose of this vaccine is not to “boost” the immune response, but to ensure the development of a protective immune response in any dog ​that may not have responded to the primary core vaccines. However, a puppy that fails to respond to any of the core primary vaccinations will be unprotected until it receives this vaccine at 12 months of age. For this reason, the World Small Animal Veterinary Association (WSAVA) Vaccination Guidelines Group (VGG) suggests that veterinarians try to reduce this possible period of susceptibility by moving the time for administering this vaccine from 52 to 26 weeks of age or any time between 26 and 52 weeks of age.4 In endemic areas puppies must also be vaccinated against rabies. The global recommendation is to give the first vaccine no earlier than 12 weeks of age with a second vaccine given 1 year later.4,11,12 ADULT DOGS Dogs that responded to vaccination with core vaccines containing MLV maintain solid immunity (immunologic memory) for several years in the absence of any repeat vaccination. Therefore, after vaccination at 6 months, subsequent revaccination should be administered at 3-year intervals.4 Canine core MLV vaccines can induce a protective immune response lasting as long as 9 years for some components and sometimes lifelong protection.14-17 An adult dog (or puppy over 26 weeks of age) with an unknown vaccination history requires only a single dose of core MLV vaccine to generate a protective immune response.4,10 Rabies vaccines can carry a 1-year or a 3-year licensed DOI. Revaccination should be based on DOI and local laws.4,9 NON-CORE VACCINES FOR DOGS The most widely used vaccines for dogs that have been designated noncore are those against Bordetella bronchiseptica, CAV-2, canine parainfluenza virus (CPiV), and leptospirosis.4,9 Other non-core vaccines with more restricted geographic availability include those against Borrelia burgdorferi, canine influenza virus (CIV), and Leishmania infantum4,9,10 (Table 185.1).

Therapies include intravenous fluids, antibiotics, antiemetics and analgesics. r Intensity depends on the severity of signs on examination. r Goals are to provide intestinal nutrients, restore and maintain fluid and electrolyte balance, and resolve shock, sepsis and endotoxemia. r Prompt, intensive in-patient care leads to treatment success. r Proper, strict isolation procedures are essential. r Exercise care to prevent the spread of CPV-2, a very stable virus. passages.text: Altering the x-ray exposure can be used to enhance visualization of certain areas, more so with film radiography than with digital radiography. Doubling the mAs increases density and contrast to enhance visualization of skeletal and mineralized structures. Cutting the exposure time in half may improve visualization of peripheral soft tissues or aid in detection of small volumes of free gas. 7. Expiratory radiographs can be used to increase lung opacity and decrease lung volume, which may aid in the detection of small volumes of gas or fluid in the pleural B A Figure 3.3  Stretching the patient. Two lateral views of the same 10-­year-­old, 22-­kg dog. In radiograph A, the patient is hyperextended resulting in dorsoventral narrowing of the thorax (double-­headed arrow), less inflated lungs, a narrowed trachea, and distortion of the cardiac silhouette. In radiograph B, the patient is in a more neutral and relaxed position, allowing the lungs to expand and producing a truer representation of the trachea and cardiac silhouette. space and cavitary lesions in the lungs. Comparing expiratory with inspiratory radiographs may be useful to evaluate suspected tracheal collapse syndrome or lung emphysema. 8. Oblique views are made with the patient rotated (Figure  2.11) and can be used to displace overlying structures away from an area of interest. For example, the heart and spine are rotated away from the esophagus in a VD oblique view. 9. Tangential beam views are made with the x-ray beam centered on a peripheral lesion in the thoracic wall or pleural space (Figure  2.12). The FOV is tightly collimated to isolate the lesion and enhance its visibility. 10. “Human view” is a VD view made with the thoracic limbs pulled caudally (Figure 2.13). It is used to eliminate superimposition of the scapula and shoulder muscles on the cranial lung lobes and mediastinum. 11. Skyline view is a craniodorsal-to-caudoventral view of the thoracic inlet (Figure 2.14). It is used to visualize the trachea in cross-section, which often aids in the evaluation of suspected tracheal collapse syndrome, tracheal stenosis, or tracheal hypoplasia. 12. Horizontal beam radiography (Figure  2.15) can be used to detect small volumes of gas or fluid in the thoracic cavity. It also can be used to reposition intra-thoracic fluid or gas to better visualize lungs or pleural space. Pleural fluid flows with gravity into the dependent part of the thoracic cavity. Gas rises to the highest or uppermost part. Radiographs of the pharynx or larynx are useful to examine the upper respiratory tract, which may be helpful in determining the etiology of lower respiratory disease.

passages.text: The thorax should be palpated for signs of trauma, rib fractures, or cardiac thrills. In cats, compressibility of the cranial thorax should be assessed, as lack thereof may suggest the presence of a cranial thoracic or mediastinal mass.18 Thoracic auscultation is of central importance. The identification of murmurs, gallops, or arrhythmias on cardiac auscultation (ch. 38) supports the presence of cardiac disease that may be responsible for respiratory distress. It is important to recognize, however, that the same geriatric small breed dogs that are predisposed to MMVD may also be predisposed to airway diseases such as chronic bronchitis or collapsing trachea, and cats may have physiologic murmurs; therefore, the presence of a heart murmur does not automatically indicate the dyspnea is cardiac in origin. Conversely, the absence of a murmur in a cat or a large breed dog does not rule out cardiac disease as the cause of dyspnea given their predisposition to cardiomyopathies. The presence of an audible gallop (third heart sound), tachycardia, and hypothermia has been demonstrated to be highly suggestive of cardiac cause for dyspnea in cats.19 Displaced or muffled heart sounds may indicate the presence of a mass, diaphragmatic hernia, and/or effusion. Pulmonary auscultation may reveal increased bronchovesicular (BV) sounds as a result of airway narrowing by constriction or secretions causing flow turbulence. Tracheal auscultation should be performed to determine whether the source of increased BV sounds is indeed the lower airways or is referred from the upper airway. Crackles or wheezes may be heard with lower airway or pulmonary parenchymal disorders. Crackles, also called rales, are discontinuous popping sounds resulting from air bubbling through fluid (not just cardiogenic edema) or from rapid opening of stiff airways. Wheezes are high-pitched continuous musical sounds indicating air movement through very narrowed airways. Decreased to absent lung sounds indicate the presence of something preventing transmission of lung sounds through the thoracic wall. If decreased ventrally, pleural effusion or a space-occupying mass may be present, whereas if decreased dorsally, pneumothorax may be present. Thoracic percussion would tend to yield dullness and increased resonance with free fluid and air, respectively. Abdominal palpation should be performed and may reveal discomfort or pain, ascites (suggesting cardiac disease, portal hypertension, neoplasia, or hypoproteinemia; ch. 21), or distension from aerophagia. Femoral pulse quality (ch. 39) may reveal additional information referable to cardiovascular status. LOCALIZATION AND DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS UPPER AIRWAY (chs. 213-215) The upper airway is composed of the nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, and extra-thoracic trachea.

passages.text: Introduction Air-filled lungs provide an excellent opacity interface to visualize intra-thoracic soft tissues. The ratio of gas to soft tissue in normally inflated lungs is greater than 10:1. To take full advantage of the gas-to-soft tissue opacity interface, make thoracic radiographs at peak inspiration. Fully inflated lungs not only enhance the visibility of intra-thoracic structures, they also separate the structures to reduce summation and superimposition artifacts (Figures  3.1 and 3.2). Poor lung inflation can mimic or mask disease. At the end of this chapter there are extensive lists of differential diagnoses for numerous radiographic findings regarding the thorax. Procedure for making thoracic radiographs 1. As needed, clean and dry the patient’s hair coat and skin prior to radiography. 2. Remove any collars, harnesses, or coverings and move any monitoring equipment out of the field-of-view (e.g., ECG leads, IV tubing). 3. Note any cutaneous or subcutaneous growths on the patient that may create artifacts in the radiographs. 4. Measure the widest part of the thorax, usually over the liver at the level of the xyphoid or 12th rib. 5. Center the x-ray beam on the heart. Landmarks include the caudal edge of the scapula or between the fourth and sixth intercostal spaces or at the point of maximum heartbeat intensity. Patients with airway obstruction may exhibit cranial lung lobe herniation (CLLH), in which the cranial aspects of the left and right cranial lung lobes herniate through the thoracic inlet during cough or increased expiratory efforts. This can be observed during physical exam as an episodic bulging or swelling at the thoracic inlet that varies with phase of respiration or that occurs during an elicited cough ( Video 212.2). CLLH is strongly correlated with dynamic intrathoracic airway collapse19 but can also occur secondary to other forms of fixed or dynamic collapse (e.g., brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome). Physical examination of the upper respiratory tract should also include an otoscopic examination, and a complete ophthalmic examination, including gentle retropulsion of the eyes to assess symmetry, as invasive nasal tumors or destructive mycotic rhinitis may extend into the orbit, and inspection of the fundus to investigate for signs of systemic or infectious diseases that may have nasal and ophthalmic manifestations (e.g., fungal infection, systemic hypertension). Physical exam findings referable to the upper airway include stertor, stridor, and decreased or absent nasal airflow ( Video 37.1). Stertor is a discontinuous, low-pitched fluttering sound that usually originates from the nasopharyngeal meatus. It is typically associated with inspiratory dysfunction, but may also be present during both phases of respiration. Because of the tendency of the nasopharyngeal meatus to narrow during rest, stertor may be more pronounced at night. Stridor is a continuous, high-pitched inspiratory sound, usually produced as a result of narrowing of the larynx or extrathoracic trachea. In contrast to stertor, stridorous respiratory noise may be absent at rest, but exacerbated by high airway flows (exercise, panting, etc.). Physical exam findings referable to the lower airways include adventitious sounds (wheezes, crackles) as well as changes in the character of normal bronchovesicular sounds. Normal inspiratory flow reaches peak velocity near the end of inspiration, while normal expiratory flow reaches peak velocity near the beginning of the expiratory phase. For this reason, thoracic auscultation of normal air flow is typically loudest at end inspiration and early expiration. Normal bronchovesicular sounds detected via auscultation are primarily generated by laminar flow through the larger central airways, and are filtered by the alveoli, pleural space, and chest wall. Changes in the volume (increased or decreased) or pattern of bronchovesicular sounds can be an early indicator of respiratory disease, even in the absence of adventitious lung sounds. Increased detection of bronchovesicular sounds can occur as a result of increased respiratory effort or pulmonary edema of any cause.

passages.text: The clinician can more effectively treat irrevocably blind eyes by identifying the cause of the glaucoma (neoplasia, lens luxation, primary angle closure, hyphema, etc.) and then performing the appropriate surgical procedure (cyclodestruction, enucleation, evisceration with intrascleral prosthesis, etc.) in conjunction with evaluating the risk of glaucoma in the remaining eye. If the affected eye has the potential for sight, however, aggressive attempts to lower IOP both medically and surgically should be instituted. In these cases the next step is to determine the inciting cause of the glaucoma and directly address that cause, if possible. Emergency Treatment of Acute Glaucoma Early identification of the cause of the glaucoma and rapid reduction of IOP are essential to prevent permanent damage. Box 12-5 summarizes emergency treatment for PACG in an eye that still has the potential for vision. Although the initial response to medical therapy may be dramatic, medical therapy alone is generally not effective in providing long-term control of IOP, and surgical therapy is often required. Reduction in pressure with this regimen is usually rapid (1 to 2 hours) but temporary (12 to 36 hours). If the eye responds to latanoprost, this medication should be continued every 12 hours until the patient can be evaluated by a specialist. In one study by Focht et al, eyes with latanoprost-responsive PACG could be controlled with this drug for an average of only 5 months before IOP rose again. If the eye is unresponsive to latanoprost, mannitol may be used, but it can be quite toxic, so its use is limited to an emergency setting in eyes with the potential for vision. If IOP remains elevated after a single injection of mannitol, the 1 g/kg dose may be repeated in 4 hours if necessary, but long-term use should be avoided. Because mannitol solution is at or near the saturation point, it may need to be heated and put through a 5 µm filter to avoid intravenous (IV) injection of crystals and potentially fatal consequences. Mannitol lowers IOP by dehydrating the vitreous along with the rest of the animal. NOTE Glaucoma is usually treated by a veterinary ophthalmologist after the family veterinarian has made the initial diagnosis and provided emergency therapy. NOTE Primary glaucoma is a bilateral disease in dogs. Once a diagnosis of glaucoma has been made in one eye, the remaining eye should receive prophylactic medication and regular pressure checks. by dividing the dose in thirds and giving it chilled or mixed with food. Glycerin is contraindicated in diabetic patients. On rare occasions glycerin may be used every 8 hours for up to 5 days if toxicity is not significant. Glycerin is occasionally dispensed for the owner to administer to treat a sudden attack of glaucoma immediately before seeking professional assistance.

Glycerin is contraindicated in diabetic patients. On rare occasions glycerin may be used every 8 hours for up to 5 days if toxicity is not significant. In addition to a systemic hyperosmotic agent, a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor such as dorzolamide 2% or brinzolamide 1% should be applied two or three times 10 minutes apart as a loading dose, then every 8 hours. If the eye also appears very congested or inflamed, intravenous administration of dexametha­ sone at 0.1 mg/kg may also be useful in the management of acute PACG. Side effects include headache, osmotic diuresis, and worsening of dehydration, renal failure, or cardiovascular disease. Deaths resulting from pulmonary edema also have been reported if mannitol is given to animals anesthetized with older gas inhalants such as methoxyflurane. A hyperosmotic agent should be used with caution if the blood–ocular barrier is not intact (uveitis, hyphema), because a leaky barrier may allow mannitol to enter the vitreous, thereby pulling water into the vitreal cavity and increasing IOP. Oral glycerin at 1 to 2 mL/kg is an alternative to mannitol, although it is a less reliable ocular hypotensive drug and frequently induces vomiting. passages.text: If the entire eye cannot be examined directly, B-scan ultrasonography is used. The corneal laceration is apposed with simple interrupted 7-0 to 8-0 absorbable sutures. To provide additional protection and support, the sutured laceration may be covered with a third eyelid flap, bulbar cortjunctival graft, or partial temporary tarsorrhaphy. Postoperative therapy to control the secondary iridocyclitis consists of topical and systemic antibiotics, systemic NSAlDs, and mydriatics. Postoperative complications include variable and often dense corneal scarring, cataract formation with posterior synechiae, secondary glaucoma, phthisis bulbus, and bacterial endophthahnitis. GLAUCOMA Animals are usually presented with high-pressure glaucoma because intraocular pressure (IOP) >40-60 mmHg results in clinical signs of buphthalmia, mydriasis, corneal edema, episcleral venous congestion, and variable ocular pain. The underlying glaucoma may be either open or narrow-closed angle, and either acute or chronic. Dog breeds most often affected with primary glaucoma include the American Cocker Spaniel, Basset Hound, Chow Chow, Akita, Chinese Shar-Pei, Norwegian Elkhound, and San1oyed. In cats, glaucoma is often associated with anterior uveitis, whereas in horses the risk factors are age > 10 yr old, anterior uveitis, and breed (Appa­ loosa). Although globe enlargement (buphthalmia) is detected fairly early in dogs, buphthalmia in horses and cats is often missed until the glaucoma has progressed. Diagnosis depends on clinical signs and accurate tonometry. The Tono-Pen® and TonoVet® applanation tonometers are the most versatile. Gonioscopy and other diagnostic methods are used to evaluate the anterior chamber angle and the posterior segment, including the optic neive head. The goals of therapy are to rapidly lower IOP and to preseive as much vision as possible. Immediate referral to a veteri­ nary ophthalmologist is often helpful. Short-term treatment includes mannitol (1-2 g/kg, IV), topical 13-blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and either prostaglandin analogues or miotics (pilocarpine or demecariun1). The beneficial effects of the topical medica­ tions are not usually apparent until IOP is <30 mm Hg. If mannitol treatment does not lower IOP within 2-4 hr, anterior chamber paracentesis under general anesthesia may be attempted. Longterm therapy usually includes topical and systemic ocular hypotensive medications, laser cyclopho­ tocoagulation, cyclocryotherapy, and anterior chamber shunts.

5) Local anaesthetic Local anaesthesia can be administered topically (e.g. proparacaine, tetracaine) or during locoregional anaesthesia (see anaesthetic). 6) Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost) This drug is used in some types of glaucoma (e.g. primary glaucoma) and contraindicated in other types of glaucoma (e.g. anterior lens luxation, uveitic glaucoma). 7) Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide) Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors should be considered to decrease intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humour production in cases of glaucoma. 8) Hyperosmotic agents (mannitol) Drugs that increase osmolality of the blood can be used intravenously to help decreasing intraocular pressure during glaucoma crisis (see anaesthetic, analgesics, sedative and emergency drugs). Complementary list 9) Agonist of cholinergic receptors/direct-acting parasympathomimetic (pilocarpine) This drug can be considered to treat neurogenic keratoconjunctivitis sicca by topical or oral administration. 10) Proteinase inhibitors Proteinase inhibitors (EDTA, N-acetylcysteine and tetracycline antibiotics) are to be considered when the activity of matrix metalloproteinases is excessive, resulting in corneal melting, which can be common in geriatric dogs. Reproduction Core list 1) Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) (Deslorelin) This is administered as subcutaneous implants. Deslorelin achieves reversible chemical sterilisation from 6 weeks post-implant and for periods of 6 months to one year in male dogs (4 years in ferrets) without significant adverse effects. 2) Antiprogestogens (Aglepristone) These drugs are used for medical interruption of pregnancy (up to 45 days after mating), induction of parturition or medical management of pyometra. Treatment is with the calcium chaimel blocker ainlodi­ pine (0.625 mg/cat once to twice daily; some cats may require 1.25 mg/cat, bid) ai1d systemic c01ticosteroids (prednisone, 0.5-1 mg/kg, PO) to help control the posterior inflai11mation. Adverse effects of ainlodipine ai·e unconunon but include azotemia, lethargy, hypokalern.ia, and tachycardia TREATMENT OF GLAUCOMA Topical medications, such as prostaglan­ dins, miotics, [3-blocking adrenergics, and topical cai·bonic anhydrase inhibitors, are the prin1aiy drugs for treatment of glaucoma (seep 497), but these are often supplemented with systemic drugs. Osmotic Diuretics: In the emergency treatment of acute glaucoma, intraoculai· pressure must be reduced urgently. This is done pharmacologically using osmotic diuretics such as maimitol or glycerol in combination witl1 other topical and systemic drugs. Osmotic diuretics are lai·ge-molecu­ lai·-weight molecules that increase the osmotic pressure of plasma relative to the aqueous and vitreous. Most of the water in the eye is in the vitreous. Dehydration of the vitreous allows the lens and iris to move posteriorly, opening tl1e iridocomeal angle. The otl1er effect is to decrease formation of aqueous hwnor. Mannitol is given ( 1-1.5 g/kg, IV over 20-30 min), witl1 tl1e effect peaking in 2-3 hr and lasting up to 5 hr. Mannitol is not metabolized and thus can be used in diabetic aninlals. Glycerol (1-2 g/kg, PO) can be used but is unpalatable, and most dogs vomit. With both drugs, water should be witllheld for 3--5 hr, and the animal should be given regular opportunities to urinate. Kidney and cardiac function should be checked before treatment, and cardiac function monitored during treatment. Mannitol can be used again within 8-12 lu· if initial control of intraocular pressure is not maintained; longtenn control is unlikely if intraocular pressures do not stay within the normal rat1ge after two treatments.

NOTE STT-1 should be performed in every ophthalmic patient, because disorders in lacrimal secretion can cause ocular surface diseases such as conjunctivitis or keratitis. Measurement of tear film osmolarity is not a commonly used test because it requires specialized and expensive instrumentation. However, it is an important tool in the diagnosis of ocular surface disorders and can be very helpful in selecting an appropriate artificial tears formulation to be used in each patient/disease. Tear film osmolarity may increase with any disorder that increases tear evaporation or decreases tear secretion. It is measured from a tear sample (as small as 0.1 µL collected without inducing reflex tearing) by means of an osmometer (Figure 9-8). As a large range of meibometry values has been reported in dogs, and because of the test’s low repeatability, meibometry is no longer considered clinically relevant in veterinary medicine. The tear film also can be evaluated in the course of the ocular surface examination, using vital stains such as fluorescein, rose bengal, and lissamine green or by using infrared ocular ther­ mography. This latter technique has demonstrated a direct correlation between STT-1 values and corneal temperature, with temperature being lower in eyes with low STT-1. Veterinary ophthalmologists also can use slit-lamp biomicroscopy to assess the tear film. The lipid layer, although difficult to appreciate clinically, may be observed as an oil-like film over the ocular surface if the eye is examined with oblique illumination and high magnification. The most common lacrimal secretory dysfunctions in domestic small animals are a deficit in one or more components of the normal tear film, usually resulting in secondary, chronic con­ junctivitis and keratitis (keratoconjunctivitis sicca [KCS]). This lacrimal secretory disease can be divided into quantitative KCS or “dry eye syndrome,” when the deficiency affects the aqueous component of the tear film; or qualitative KCS, when the quality of the tear film is diminished, usually due to lipid or mucin disorders. Quantitative Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca Quantitative KCS is a deficiency of the aqueous component of the tear film, which provides metabolic support and microbial protection to the cornea. Dry eye is a very common canine eye disease with a reported incidence of up to 2%. Conversely, the incidence of feline dry eye is very low. Etiology Quantitative KCS can be congenital or acquired, with the latter due to either ophthalmic or systemic disorders (Table 9-1). Ophthalmic causes of acquired KCS include autoimmune disease, drugs, radiation therapy, orbital or supraorbital trauma, ocular surgery, and neoplasia; systemic causes of acquired KCS include neurogenic, metabolic, or infectious disease and systemic drugs.

passages.text: A topical ophthalmic antibiotic ointment (bacitracin-polymixin-neomycin) was prescribed to be given, in both eyes, every 6–8 hours for approximately 2 weeks to control the bacterial overgrowth. Artificial tear ointment was also prescribed to be given, at least 3–4 times daily, in the right eye, to replace tear film. A recheck visit was scheduled for 4 weeks to re-evaluate the eye, perform another Schirmer tear test, and to evaluate the response to the treatment. The owner was instructed to keep the eyes clean and free of dried discharge; the eyes should be cleaned multiple times throughout the day with warm water and a washcloth. Discussions about the importance of keeping the eye well lubricated is essential to prevent corneal ulcerations. The owner was told to contact the hospital if Lulu is experiencing ocular pain or if the mucopurulent discharge persists after 1 week. KCS causes inflammation of the cornea and surrounding tissues due to inadequate production of the aqueous portion of the tear film by the lacrimal gland. Immune-mediated causes are the most common and the patient’s immune system is attacking the lacrimal glands which is affecting tear production. Prognosis: KCS is usually life-long, chronic disease that is usually controllable but not often curable. Eyes that respond to tear stimulants have a good prognosis. Lulu was diagnosed early and no corneal ulcers or scarring was observed. TECHNICIAN NOTES Clients must be warned about the potential side effects of metronidazole, at higher dosages, including neurologic toxicity (Plumb, 2015). Corticosteroids Corticosteroids exert antiinflammatory and immunosuppressive effects through their inhibitory influence on neutrophils, T lymphocytes, blood vessels (decreased permeability), and cellular messengers (e.g., prostaglandin). They are generally considered to be antiinflammatory at lower doses and immunosuppressive at higher doses. Corticosteroids are often used in combination with other immunosuppressant/antineoplastic agents. Other Immunosuppressive Agents • Tacrolimus (Protopic). This is a topical agent that may be used in the treatment of atopic dermatitis and other dermatologic conditions. It is both an antiinflammatory and an immunosuppressant. • Pimecrolimus (Elidel). This is a topical agent similar to tacrolimus. • Oclacitinib (Apoquel). This agent is a janus kinase inhibitor labeled for the control of pruritus in dogs older than 12 months of age. • Mycophenolate mofetil. This is an immunosuppressive drug that may be used for treating immune-mediated hemolytic anemia, inflammatory bowel disease, or myasthenia gravis in dogs.

Three times a day therapy has been employed during the initial phases of treatment in more difficult or slow responding cases. For unknown reasons (reversal of lacrimal adenitis > reorganization of lacrimal epithelial cell function > formation of secretory granules > tear production) 3–8 weeks of therapy are necessary before a dramatic increase in the Schirmer tear test becomes evident. Patients are generally maintained for life on cyclosporine ophthalmic once or twice daily depending on the response. Discontinuation of therapy is usually associated with the return of clinical signs of KCS within a few days. Reinstitution of therapy, at this time, is usually associated with an almost immediate return of tear production (versus the initial lag phase noted). This likely is related to the degree of inflammatory disease noted with short discontinuation of therapy versus that present initially, prior to the diagnosis of KCS. If tear production is very low, cyclosporine is often used in combination with artificial tears during the initial phases of therapy. Once tear production is improved, artificial tears can generally be removed completely or their frequency reduced in the treatment plan. After treatment is initiated, reevaluation of tear production in one month is recommended. If ulcerative keratitis complicates keratoconjunctivitis sicca in the dog, more frequent evaluation is necessary. Cyclosporine, although an immunomodulating agent, is considered safe in the face of ulcerative keratitis, with concurrent antibiotic therapy. Caution is advised, however. When cyclosporine is delivered topically, no systemic toxicity has been noted in dogs given this drug chronically. This is probably associated with the poor absorption of this drug across the GI tract and because it is delivered to the eye at very low concentrations which even if 100% absorbed, when divided over the body weight of the dog is well below even the therapeutic dose. Advanced detection methods have made it possible to measure trace levels of cyclosporine in the blood of dogs being topically treated for dry eye. The clinical implication of this finding is uncertain at this time. Dosage Forms/Regulatory Status Optimmune® ointment is the approved formulation of topical cyclosporine for the management of dry eye in dogs. Compounding of topical cyclosporine drops was popular before the introduction, approval, and marketing of Optimmune® ointment. Clinicians persistently using compounded formulations of cyclosporine eye drops may be outside of expected ethical and legal standards of practice except under very specific situations. The use of commercially available ophthalmic products instead of compounded medications is highly recommended. Optimmune® is first applied 2 or 3 times daily and frequency of daily application is adjusted based on clinical response. TREATMENT r Outpatient—unless secondary severe corneal ulceration. r Inform client that medical therapy is generally life-long. r When solutions and ointments are prescribed, instruct client to use the solution(s) before the ointment(s) and wait at least 5 minutes between treatments. r Advise client to call at once if ocular pain increases because patients are predisposed to corneal ulceration. r Parotid duct transposition—surgical procedure that reroutes the parotid duct to deliver saliva to the ocular surface if KCS is refractory to lacrimogenic therapy; more common with congenital KCS; saliva can be irritating to the cornea and result in mineral deposits; some patients require ongoing topical medical therapy. passages.text: Respiratory system involvement is usually indicative of moderate to severe anaphylaxis with signs of bronchoconstriction, upper airway edema, and/or bronchorrhea: tachypnea, bradypnea, dyspnea, wheezing, coughing, cyanosis, stridor, stertor, and/or respiratory arrest (ch. 123).5,10,16 Life-threatening anaphylaxisinduced respiratory effects have been noted in about 67% of affected dogs and cats.6,16 It is difficult to interpret respiratory signs in the retrospective studies, as tachypnea or open-mouth breathing can be caused by stress, pain, or hypotension. DIAGNOSIS The diagnosis of anaphylaxis (Figure 129.1) is dependent on consistent history and clinicopathologic findings. The history may reveal previous anaphylactic events or recent exposure to an insect sting, vaccination, or new medication. There may have been prior exposure to blood products. While increases in serum histamine and tryptase concentrations are useful diagnostic markers in people, their concentrations rise and abate rapidly, sensitivity and specificity are modest, and serial measurements are recommended.19,21 These tests are not readily available to veterinarians, and their clinical utility has yet to be established in small animals. TREATMENT INITIAL TREATMENT AND USE OF EPINEPHRINE The life-threatening nature of anaphylaxis demands rapid intervention, constant monitoring, and immediate vascular access (ch. 119). Treatment should focus on airway patency, breathing, and circulation. Removing any exposure to the inciting cause, if possible, is critical (Figure 129.2). Multiple sources emphasize using epinephrine in treating anaphylaxis.1,22 The adrenergic effects include decreased mediator release from mast cells and basophils, vasoconstriction, positive inotropy and chronotropy, bronchodilation, and decreased mucosal edema, which assists with upper airway obstructions.22 Following the onset of hypotension in a group of dogs with experimentally induced anaphylactic shock, constant rate intravenous (IV) infusion of epinephrine was superior to bolus dosing subcutaneously, intramuscularly, or intravenously.23 Significant amounts of epinephrine may be required in hypotensive patients. If bolus dosing is implemented, a subsequent infusion should be titrated to effect (Figure 129.2).20 As infusion rates vary, toxic effects can develop as the anaphylaxis resolves, demanding careful monitoring of pets receiving an infusion.20 Epinephrine autoinjectors for out-of-hospital use are available but doses are too large for dogs under 15 kg. In many parts of the world autoinjectors may be expensive. An alternative may be pre-filled light-protected syringes, which have been shown to maintain stability and sterility for up to 90 days.24 Bespoke doses, likely safer than an owner drawing from a vial in a time of crisis, may be prescribed.

(Corley 2003) RUMINANTS, SWINE: For treatment of anaphylaxis: a) 0.5–1 mL/100 lbs. body weight of 1:1,000 SC or IM; dilute to 1:10,000 if using IV; may be repeated at 15 minute intervals Often used in conjunction with corticosteroids and diphenhydramine (Clark 1986) Monitoring Cardiac rate/rhythm Respiratory rate/auscultation during anaphylaxis Urine flow, if possible Blood pressure and blood gases, if indicated and possible Client Information Pre-loaded syringes containing an appropriate amount of epinephrine may be dispensed to clients for treatment of anaphylaxis in animals with known hypersensitivity. Anaphylactic clinical signs (depending on species) should be discussed. Clients should be instructed in proper injection technique (IM or SC) and storage conditions for epinephrine. Do not use epinephrine if it is outdated, discolored, or contains a precipitate.

If bolus dosing is implemented, a subsequent infusion should be titrated to effect (Figure 129.2).20 As infusion rates vary, toxic effects can develop as the anaphylaxis resolves, demanding careful monitoring of pets receiving an infusion.20 Epinephrine autoinjectors for out-of-hospital use are available but doses are too large for dogs under 15 kg. In many parts of the world autoinjectors may be expensive. An alternative may be pre-filled light-protected syringes, which have been shown to maintain stability and sterility for up to 90 days.24 Bespoke doses, likely safer than an owner drawing from a vial in a time of crisis, may be prescribed. Use of outof-hospital epinephrine is at clinician’s discretion and may be considered. Atropine may also be indicated for hypotension coupled with bradycardia. FIGURE 129.2  Anaphylaxis action plan. BP, Blood pressure; ECG, electrocardiogram; EPI, epinephrine; ETCO2, end tidal carbon dioxide; IM, intramuscular; IV, intravenous; SpO2, peripheral oxygen saturation. Modified from Brown SG. Anaphylaxis: clinical concepts and research priorities. Emerg Med Australas. 2006;18(2):155-169. INTRAVENOUS FLUIDS Large-volume IV fluid bolus using a balanced isotonic crystalloid may be required to combat hypotension (ch. 120). Careful reassessment of the patient following each fluid challenge should focus on heart rate, mucous membrane color, capillary refill time, pulse quality, mentation, peripheral temperature, and blood pressure. Fresh frozen plasma or red blood cells may be required if hemorrhage or coagulopathy exist.7,16 IV glucose should be administered immediately for hypoglycemia ( Video 61.3) and monitored (chs. 61 and 289; Figure 129.2). ANTIHISTAMINES AND GLUCOCORTICOIDS (CH. 143) Antihistamines are not a frontline treatment for life-threatening anaphylaxis and should not delay better immediate treatments. Cardiovascular responses observed in dogs with experimentally induced anaphylaxis were not prevented by pretreatment with antihistamines.25 A Cochrane systematic review of H1 antihistamines was unable to identify any quality evidence for their use.26 Potential harmful effects may be observed with some antihistamines: promethazine possesses vasodilatory effects, and rapid chlorpheniramine infusion may cause hypotension and should be avoided in severe reactions.1,27 Antihistamines may be useful to alleviate pruritus and wheals in mild reactions. While glucocorticoids are commonly utilized, evidence for their use is lacking.1 Their delayed onset of action, regardless of route of administration, limits usefulness during the hyperacute phase.

The results of the CBC, serum biochemistry profile, and urinalysis are often within normal limits in dogs with pancreatitis, especially in those dogs with mild pancreatitis.3 However, dogs with pancreatitis may present with almost any hematological or biochemical abnormality.3 Different combinations of increases in liver enzyme activities (i.e., alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase; ch. 65) and hyperbilirubinemia are common and, when present, should raise the suspicion for pancreatitis.3 In some cases, these findings might be associated with extrahepatic biliary tract obstruction (chs. 272, 273). Increases in serum creatinine, urea nitrogen, and/or symmetric dimethylarginine concentrations (ch. 62) are variably present and most often associated with dehydration, but may also point to secondary kidney injury. Other possible findings include hypertriglyceridemia, hypercholesterolemia (ch. 63), hypoalbuminemia (ch. 60), and hyperglycemia (sometimes associated with diabetes) or hypoglycemia (ch. 61).3,6 A variety of electrolyte abnormalities may also be present in dogs with pancreatitis, with hypokalemia being the most common (ch. 68). LABORATORY TESTS FOR PANCREATITIS Pancreatic Lipase Immunoreactivity (PLI) PLI is currently considered the most sensitive and specific serum test for the diagnosis of pancreatitis in dogs. The main advantage of PLI assays over traditional lipase activity assays is specificity. In contrast to traditional assays for lipase activity, which indiscriminately measure the activities of lipases of multiple cellular origins, immunoassays exclusively quantify lipase of pancreatic origin based on its unique 3-dimensional structure.7,8 Therefore, PLI assays have inherent advantages over the traditional serum lipase activity assays that make them more suitable for specific evaluation of the exocrine pancreas in dogs and cats. Available Assays The originally developed and analytically validated immunoassays for the specific measurement of serum pancreatic lipase in dogs (canine PLI [cPLI])9 have been replaced by a more widely available, fully validated assay (Spec cPL) that demonstrates a similar clinical performance to the original PLI assays and is available through IDEXX Laboratories and the Gastrointestinal Laboratory at Texas A&M University.10 The reference interval for Spec cPL is 0 to 200 mcg/L. Concentrations ≥400 mcg/L (Spec cPL) are considered highly suggestive of pancreatitis. A rapid, in-clinic, semiquantitative assay for the estimation of canine pancreatic lipase in serum (SNAP cPL) is also available.11 The results of this rapid assay are considered either normal or abnormal. Dogs with a “normal” result are unlikely to have pancreatitis, whereas those with an “abnormal” result might have pancreatitis or a Spec cPL in the equivocal range.11 However, the two cannot be differentiated without quantitative evaluation by measurement of a

passages.chapter: 277. Pancreatitis in Dogs: Diagnosis and Management

passages.text: Abnormal findings potentially due to pancreatitis can also be caused by frequently diagnosed comorbid disease(s) or complications. The most common clinical signs include lethargy (incidence: 51-100%) and inappetence (62-97%). Vomiting (35-52%) and weight loss (30-47%) are frequent. Diarrhea (11-38%), dyspnea (6-20%), and polydipsia/polyuria (PU/PD; 20%) are less common and often caused by non-pancreatic conditions. Dehydration (37-92%), hypothermia (39-68%), and/or hyperthermia/fever (7-26%) are common. Fever is more common with acute pancreatitis or pancreatic complications. Apparent abdominal pain is only reported in 10-30% of cases, but identifying pain in cats is challenging.8,21 Resistance to direct pancreatic palpation or to transducer pressure during ultrasound (US) examination may be indicative of pain. Icterus (6-37%) and/or cranial abdominal mass/organomegaly (4-23%) in cats with pancreatitis can lead to a non-pancreatic disease being prioritized.3,8,12,22-24 The clinical signs of pancreatitis are based on retrospective studies in cats with severe forms of acute pancreatitis. Thus, the clinical signs in less severe or more chronic pancreatitis are likely even less specific and more obscure. DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC), SERUM BIOCHEMISTRY PROFILE, URINALYSIS (UA) After obtaining a medical history, including drug history, and performing a PE, results of a CBC, biochemistry profile, and UA are valuable for cats with clinical signs consistent with pancreatitis. These test results permit screening for differential diagnoses, pancreatic complications, and comorbidities.2 Abnormalities are unpredictable. Hemoconcentration (17% of cats) secondary to dehydration and an inflammatory leukogram characterized by neutrophilia (46%) with a left shift or neutropenia (15%) may be present, particularly with severe acute pancreatitis. Non-regenerative anemia (38%) can be present, particularly with chronic pancreatitis. Thrombocytopenia is rare in cats with severe acute pancreatitis associated with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).2 Increases in liver enzyme activities (alanine transaminase 57%; alkaline phosphatase 49%) and hyperbilirubinemia (58%) may be present due to cholangitis, extrahepatic bile duct obstruction (ch. 273), and/or hepatic lipidosis (ch. 274).2 Hyperglycemia (45%), associated with relative or absolute insulin deficiency, and, less frequently, hypoglycemia (associated with a poor outcome),4 can be seen with acute necrotizing pancreatitis.4,12 Increases in blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and symmetric dimethylarginine can be secondary to dehydration, but when persistent or associated with inappropriate urine concentration, may indicate acute kidney injury (AKI).
