Renal Azotemia Acute or chronic kidney diseases (primary kidney disease affecting glomeruli, renal tubules, renal interstitium, and/or renal vasculature) that impair at least 75% of kidney function (glomerular filtration rate). RISK FACTORS r Medical conditions—kidney disease, hypoadrenocorticism, low cardiac output, hypotension, fever, sepsis, polyuria, liver disease, pyometra, hypoalbuminemia, dehydration, acidosis, exposure to nephrotoxic chemicals, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, urolithiasis, urethral plugs in cats, urethral trauma, and neoplasia. r Advanced age may be a risk factor. r Drugs—potentially nephrotoxic drugs, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, diuretics, antihypertensive medications; failure to adjust dosage of drugs primarily eliminated by the kidneys to correspond with decline in renal function.

passages.text: Keep in mind that with diseases that cause pre-renal azotemia, prolonged reduction in renal blood flow can eventually cause renal damage secondary to renal hypoxia, leading to acute kidney injury (AKI) and thereby adding a renal cause to the current azotemia (ch. 300). Broad mechanisms of reduced renal blood flow and thereby decreased GFR include hypovolemia, decreased cardiac output, and altered vasomotor tone leading to poor renal perfusion. Causes of hypovolemia include dehydration, hemorrhage, shock, or loss of fluids through mechanisms such as vomiting, diarrhea, thirdspacing, hypoadrenocorticism, and severe burns (ch. 119). Causes of decreased cardiac output include cardiomyopathies (such as dilated cardiomyopathy), sepsis, severe brady- or tachyarrhythmias, anaphylaxis, and hypoadrenocorticism. Causes of altered vascular tone primarily include sepsis and anaphylaxis. Despite pre-renal azotemia being commonly viewed as a correctable problem, recent data from human medicine has suggested a change in terminology to “volume-responsive acute kidney injury” since these patients have worse outcomes despite the absence of a renal source of azotemia (ch. 300).20,21 Further investigation is warranted to know if this finding is applicable to veterinary species, although initial investigations utilizing this terminology have begun.22,23 BLOOD UREA NITROGEN (BUN) TO SERUM CREATININE (sCR) RATIOS Because there is a significant amount of urea reabsorption from the tubules, especially in times of low tubular flow rate, BUN can increase earlier and with a higher magnitude than creatinine. This can be demonstrated by the BUN/sCr ratio; however, there are too many factors that can alter this ratio to make it clinically relevant. SDMA-SPECIFIC CONSIDERATIONS There are minimal data specifically addressing the use of SDMA in pre-renal causes of biomarker elevation. Because SDMA is a more sensitive marker for decreased GFR, its circulating concentration will also be elevated along with BUN and sCr, but to date there are no studies to suggest additional benefit of measuring SDMA along with the traditional markers of azotemia. RENAL CAUSES OF BIOMARKER CHANGES Any disease process that results in reduction of renal functional mass will cause reduction of GFR over time and ultimately azotemia. Previous studies have documented an approximate 75% reduction in renal functional mass necessary to result in azotemia.24-26 Azotemia typically occurs after loss of concentrating ability of the renal tubules, thereby resulting in an inadequate USG for the patient’s current volume and hydration status. However, one study documents that this relationship may not always be true in cats that can retain concentrating ability despite the presence of renal azotemia.27,28 Categorical causes include loss of nephrons, decreased glomerular patency, increased interstitial pressure, increased intratubular pressure, or intravascular obstructive lesions.

When target cells in the kidney lack the biochemical machinery necessaiy to respond to the secretion of n01mal or increased circulating levels of ADH, nephrogenic diabetes insipid us results. PRIMARY POLYURIA Overview Arginine vasopressin (AVP; antidiuretic hormone [ADH]) is the main hormone responsible for water homeostasis, acting within renal collecting ducts to increase cell permeability to water. AVP stimulates osmotic reabsorption of water from the hypotonic tubular lumen into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, from which it is returned to the circulation. Disrupting any of these steps can lead to PU and secondary PD (PU causes PD). Secondary PD is an essential physiological response to avoid volume depletion and osmotic consequences. Diabetes Insipidus (DI): Central and Nephrogenic Central DI (CDI; ch. 282) is a condition resulting from complete or partial deficiencies in AVP and can be due to neoplasia, inflammation, trauma, or developmental defects.5,6 Some cases are idiopathic. Absolute AVP deficiencies are more commonly diagnosed, perhaps because the PU/PD is profound. Nephrogenic DI (NDI) is defined as a complete or partial inability of the kidneys to respond to AVP. Primary NDI is a rare hereditary disorder that results in severe PU/PD at an early age.7 Secondary NDI, the most common cause of PU/PD in small animals, is caused by several diseases and can be the result of drugs that cause hyposthenuria, isosthenuria or minimally concentrated urine specific gravity (USG). Disruption of the Osmotic Gradient The abnormal presence of osmotically active agents in the renal tubular lumen can disrupt the osmotic gradient and impair water reabsorption.

passages.text: Congenital and Developmental Renal Diseases C BASICS DEFINITION r Functional or morphologic abnormalities resulting from heritable (genetic) or acquired disease processes affecting differentiation and growth of the developing kidney before or shortly after birth. r Renal agenesis— complete absence of one or both kidneys. r Renal dysplasia—disorganized renal parenchymal development. r Renal ectopia—congenital malposition of one or both kidneys; ectopic kidneys may be fused. r Glomerulopathy—glomerular disease of any type. r Tubulointerstitial nephropathy—a non-inflammatory disorder of renal tubules and interstitium. r Polycystic renal disease—formation of multiple, variable-sized cysts throughout the renal medulla and cortex. r Renal telangiectasia—multifocal vascular malformations involving the kidneys and other organs. r Renal amyloidosis— extracellular deposition of amyloid in glomerular capillaries, glomeruli, and interstitium. r Nephroblastoma—a congenital renal neoplasm arising from the pluripotent metanephric blastema. r Multifocal renal cystadenocarcinoma—a hereditary renal neoplasm in dogs. r Fanconi syndrome—a generalized renal tubular functional anomaly characterized by impaired reabsorption of glucose, phosphate, electrolytes, amino acids, and uric acid. r Primary renal glucosuria—an isolated functional defect in renal tubular reabsorption of glucose. r Cystinuria—excessive urinary excretion of cystine because of an isolated functional defect in renal tubular reabsorption of cystine and other dibasic amino acids. r Xanthinuria—excessive urinary excretion of xanthine caused by a deficiency in xanthine oxidase. r Hyperuricuria—excessive urinary excretion of uric acid, sodium urate, or ammonium urate. r Primary hyperoxaluria— intermittent hyperoxaluria, l-glyceric aciduria, oxalate nephropathy, and acute renal failure. r Congenital nephrogenic diabetes insipidus—polyuria caused by diminished renal responsiveness to antidiuretic hormone. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY r Many congenital and developmental renal disorders are caused by genetic abnormalities that disrupt the normal sequential and coordinated development and interaction of multiple embryonic tissues involved in formation of the mature kidney. r Congenital and developmental renal disorders may also be caused by non-genetic factors affecting the developing kidney before or shortly after birth. SYSTEMS AFFECTED Renal/Urologic GENETICS r Familial renal disorders have been reported in the following breeds of dogs and cats: ◦Renal agenesis in beagle and Doberman pinscher ◦Renal dysplasia in Alaskan malamute, border terrier, boxer, chow chow, Dutch kookier, golden retriever, keeshond, Lhasa apso, miniature schnauzer, Rhodesian ridgeback, shih tzu, soft-coated Wheaten terrier, and standard poodle dogs ◦Glomerulopathy in beagle, Belgian shepherd, Bernese mountain dog, Brittany spaniel, bull terrier, bullmastiff, Dalmatian, Doberman pinscher, English cocker spaniel, Newfoundland, Pembroke Welsh corgi, rottweiler, Samoyed, and soft-coated Wheaten terrier dogs ◦Tubulointerstitial nephropathy in Norwegian elkhound dogs ◦Polycystic renal disease in beagle, bull terrier, cairn terrier, and West Highland white terrier dogs, and in Persian, exotic shorthair, and Himalayan cats ◦Renal telangiectasia in Pembroke Welsh corgi ◦Renal amyloidosis in Abyssinian, Oriental shorthair, and Siamese cats, and in beagle, English foxhound, and shar-pei dogs ◦Renal cystadenocarcinoma in German shepherds ◦Fanconi syndrome in basenji and border terrier dogs ◦Primary renal glucosuria in Norwegian elkhound, Scottish terrier, and basenji dogs ◦Cystinuria in Australian cattle, Australian shepherd, basenji, basset hound, bullmastiff, Chihuahua, English bulldog, dachshund, French bulldog, Irish terrier, mastiff, Newfoundland, Scottish deer hound, Staffordshire bull terrier, and Welsh corgi dogs and in domestic cats ◦Xanthinuria in Cavalier King Charles spaniel and wirehaired dachshund dogs, and in domestic shorthair cats ◦Hyperuricuria in Dalmatians, black Russian terriers, and English bulldogs ◦Primary hyperoxaluria in domestic shorthair cats and in Tibetan spaniels.

Orient the incision parallel to the linea alba to facilitate visualization during suturing of the aborad then orad sides of the gastropexy. The gastropexy may be done by hand with intracorporeal knot tying or using an automatic suture assist device (Endostitch, Autosuture, Tyco Healthcare Inc., Norwalk, Connecticut). Mini-laparotomy prophylactic gastropexy. Place the dog in left lateral recumbency. Make a 6-cm vertical skin the serosal surface of the stomach incorporated by the hori­ zontal mattress suture. Place three more horizontal mattress sutures through the body wall and coagulated region of the stomach, separating each by 2 to 2.5 cm. Reduce abdomi­ nal insufflation and secure the sutures to form a gastropexy. Close the portal sites routinely. Intracorporeally Sutured Laparoscopic Gastro­ pexy. A technique for intracorporeally sutured laparo­ scopic gastropexy was recently reported (Mayhew and Brown, 2009). Place an initial endoscope port in the infra­ umbilical site. Establish two instrument ports on the ventral midline with one 3- to 4-cm caudal to the xiphoid process and the second midway between the established ports on midline. Move the endoscope to the middle port. Place a FIG 20-82. A, Positioning for endoscopically assisted gastropexy as described in the literature with the endoscopist positioned to the patient’s left and the surgeon at the patient’s dorsum. B, Alternatively, the endoscopist may be at the patient’s head and the monitor to the patient’s left. Strict adherence to asepsis must be maintained with \ the monitor positioned adjacent to the surgery site. Surgeon Endoscopist Monitor Light from the endoscope Incision Surgeon Endoscopist Monitor A B proper placement of the gastric incision. Make a 3-cm lon­ gitudinal incision through the serosa and muscularis layers of the gastric antrum approximately 5 cm orad to the pylorus (Fig. 20-83, C). Beginning at the dorsal edge, suture the edges of the incision to the abdominal muscles using a simple continuous suture pattern (Fig. 20-83, D). Close the muscles, subcutaneous tissues, and skin routinely. HEALING OF THE STOMACH The extraordinarily rich blood supply, reduced bacterial numbers (caused by gastric acidity), rapidly regenerating epithelium, and defense mechanisms provided by the omentum allow gastric incisions to heal quickly.

Incise the skin approxi­ mately 4 cm over the coagulated region of the body wall under endoscopic guidance. Pass four metric PDS sutures on a 36-mm, half-circle needle through the body wall and seromuscular layer of the stomach in a mattress pattern exiting the body wall through the skin incision. Coagulate dog’s spine and the endoscopist positioned at the dog’s ventrum (Fig. 20-82), pass the flexible endoscope into the stomach, and insufflate until rugal folds are minimized. An assistant may be required to manually occlude the cervical esophagus during insufflation. Palpate and indent the body wall caudal to the 13th rib and stomach at the proposed gastropexy site at the pyloric antrum. Pass polypropylene suture (0 or 2-0) percutaneously in a mattress suture fashion through the skin, body wall, pyloric antrum, and back through the body wall and skin. Temporarily tighten the suture with hemostatic forceps and place another suture in the same manner 4 to 5 cm aborad to the first suture. These stay sutures guide the paracostal approach for the gastro­ pexy, which is approached as for the laparoscopic-assisted gastropexy. Incise the seromuscular layer of the pyloric antrum and suture it to the transversus abdominis muscle in two simple continuous patterns avoiding the stay sutures. Remove the stay sutures and close the external abdominal FIG 20-81. For a laparoscopic gastropexy, A, Place the first cannula just caudal to the umbilicus and place the second cannula just right of midline, approximately 2 to 4 cm behind the last rib (make this incision parallel to the rib). B, Pull the stomach out through the incision. C, Place stay sutures between it and the body wall. Perform a gastropexy as described in Figure 20-79. A B mattress suture (2-0 nonabsorbable monofilament) through the body wall 2 to 3 cm caudal to the last rib and 5 to 8 cm lateral to the linea alba on the right side of the abdomen. Take a full-thickness bite of the pyloric antrum and exit through the body wall adjacent to the entry site. Incise the transversus abdominis and seromuscular layer of the stomach at the gastropexy site. Orient the incision parallel to the linea alba to facilitate visualization during suturing of the aborad then orad sides of the gastropexy. The gastropexy may be done by hand with intracorporeal knot tying or using an automatic suture assist device (Endostitch, Autosuture, Tyco Healthcare Inc., Norwalk, Connecticut).

Sedation (pure mu opioids [e.g., methadone 0.2-0.5 mg/kg IV, hydromorphone 0.05-0.02 mg/kg, or fentanyl 3.5 mcg/kg], combined with midazolam 0.1-0.5 mg/kg IV) is generally necessary to facilitate passage of the orogastric tube. Due to patient intolerance, risk for gastric rupture, and the risk of aspiration pneumonia, the author prefers percutaneous trocarisation as the primary mode of gastric decompression. Monitoring of vital parameters, blood pressure, and electrolyte and acid-base status should be performed as frequently as needed based on the severity of abnormalities in the patient being presented. Once the patient is hemodynamically stable and gastric decompression has been performed, the patient is anesthetized for abdominal exploratory surgery, resection of compromised tissues, and gastropexy. Dogs undergoing surgery >3 hours post-admission have a poorer prognosis, so rapid stabilization and surgical intervention are indicated.101 The postoperative management of GDV patients includes alleviating pain (ch. 6) and addressing the sequelae of poor tissue perfusion and ischemia-reperfusion injury, including electrolyte imbalances, ventricular arrhythmias, GI ulceration, systemic inflammatory response syndrome, acute kidney injury, and DIC.108 Serial monitoring of lactate, especially in dogs with high blood lactate at admission, may be helpful in determining prognosis and monitoring response to surgery and postoperative treatment.101,109 Affected dogs should also be monitored for the development of septic peritonitis through serial abdominal ultrasonography and evaluation of abdominal effusion (ch. 265). GDV PROPHYLAXIS Gastropexy is recommended for all dogs that are being surgically managed for GDV as well as at-risk dogs undergoing abdominal surgery for other reasons (e.g., ovariohysterectomy, foreign object removal, splenectomy) to minimize the risk of future volvulus. A variety of surgical fixation approaches (i.e., endoscopic-assisted, laparoscopic-assisted, and via laparotomy) and techniques (i.e., incisional, belt-loop, circumcostal) has been described. Gastropexy is performed on the right side of the abdomen, near the last rib. There is no “gold-standard” technique and surgeon preference and available equipment generally guide the approach. However, the placement of the gastropexy site is critical to minimize the risk of complications, such as partial pyloric outflow obstruction.110 Alteration of feeding behavior, including moistening wet food, feeding smaller volumes more frequently, avoiding feeding from a raised position, and using feeding devices to slow eating might also help to minimize the risk of gastric dilatation and GDV. Gastropexy does not remove the risk of gastric dilatation and approximately 511% of dogs will have recurrent gastric dilatation following gastropexy; thus, concurrent nutritional management in these dogs may be critical to successful long-term outcome.111,112 References 1.

passages.text: gastroparalysis [gas″tro-pә-ral′ә-sis] paralysis of the stomach; gastroplegia. gastropathy [gas-trop′ә-the] any disease of the stomach. chronic hypertrophic pyloric g. see antral pyloric hypertrophy syndrome. gastropexy [gas′tro-pek″se] surgical ﬁxation of the stomach, most commonly to the abdominal wall as a means of preventing recurrence of gastric volvulus. belt-loop g. a modiﬁcation of the circumcostal technique in which the seromuscular gastric ﬂap is passed around a loop of transverse abdominal muscle instead of a rib. circumcostal g. ﬁxation by a ﬂap of gastric serosa and muscularis anchored around a rib. permanent incisional g. edges of an incision into the seromuscular layers of the pyloric antrum are sutured to an incision into the peritoneum and internal fascia of the rectus abdominal or transverse abdominal muscles. tube g. a method using a Foley catheter placed in the pyloric antrum and through the abdominal wall in the right paracostal area during the postsurgical period. Gastrophilus [gas-trof′ĭ-lәs] see Gasterophilus. gastrophrenic [gas″tro-fren′ik] pertaining to the stomach and diaphragm. g. ligament part of the greater omentum that binds the left crus of the diaphragm to the fundus of the stomach. gastroplasty [gas′tro-plas″te] plastic repair of the stomach. gastroplegia [gas″tro-ple′jә] gastroparalysis. gastroplication [gas″tro-plĭ-ka′shәn] treatment of gastric dilatation by stitching a fold in the stomach wall. Often used to invaginate and suture a section of stomach wall with questionable viability into the stomach, as an alternative to partial gastrectomy in the management of gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV). gastropod [gas′tro-pod] members of the class Gastropoda; slugs and snails. gastroprotectant [gas″tro-pro-tek′tənt] see gastric protectant. gastroptosis [gas″trop-to′sis, gas″tro-to′sis] downward displacement of the stomach. gastropulmonary [gas″tro-pool′mo-nar-e] pertaining to the stomach and lungs. gastropylorectomy [gas″tro-pi″lә-rek′tә-me] excision of the pyloric part of the stomach. gastropyloric [gas″tro-pi-lor′ik] pertaining to the stomach and pylorus.

gastroptosis [gas″trop-to′sis, gas″tro-to′sis] downward displacement of the stomach. gastropulmonary [gas″tro-pool′mo-nar-e] pertaining to the stomach and lungs. gastropylorectomy [gas″tro-pi″lә-rek′tә-me] excision of the pyloric part of the stomach. gastropyloric [gas″tro-pi-lor′ik] pertaining to the stomach and pylorus. gastrorrhagia [gas″tro-ra′jә] hemorrhage from the stomach. gastrorrhaphy [gas-tror′ә-fe] suture of the stomach. gastrorrhea [gas″tro-re′ә] excessive secretion by the glands of the stomach. gastroschisis [gas-tros′kĭ-sis] a congenital ﬁssure of the abdominal wall. gastroscope [gas′tro-skōp] a ﬂexible endoscope used to examine the lumen of the stomach. gastroscopy [gas-tros′kә-pe] endoscopic examination of the lumen of the stomach. gastrospasm [gas′tro-spaz″әm] spasm of the stomach. gastrosplenic [gas″tro-splen′ik] pertaining to the stomach and spleen; gastrolienal. gastrostaxis [gas″tro-stak′sis] the oozing of blood from the stomach mucosa. gastrostenosis [gas″tro-stә-no′sis] contraction or shrinkage of the stomach. gastrostogavage [gas-tros″to-gә-vahzh′] feeding through a gastric ﬁstula. gastrostolavage [gas-tros″to-lә-vahzh′] irrigation of the stomach through a gastric ﬁstula. gastrostomy [gas-tros′tә-me] the creation of an opening into the stomach. blind g. placement of a gastric feeding tube without laparotomy or endoscope, simply by manipulating the end of the tube through the stomach and body wall. low proﬁle g. tube (device) consists of an internal mushroom or balloon tip, a short shaft connecting to an external stabilizer and a one-way antireﬂux valve with a connector for the feeding equipment. It avoids the long, external tube that is less well accepted by the dog and owner. percutaneous endoscopic g. (PEG) used for placement of a gastric feeding tube. An endoscope is used to position an incision through the body wall and stomach wall, to grasp and withdraw a suture inserted through the opening and to guide the placement of the tube that is pulled back into the stomach and through the opening by traction on the suture that has been attached to the distal end of the tube.

Antiemetic agents (metoclopra­ mide at 0.2-0.5 mg/kg, SC, or 1-2 mg/kg/day, constant-rate IV infusion; ma.ropitant at 1 mg/kg/day, SC) may be administered in cases of continued vomiting. Postoperative cardiac arrhythmias are common, but treatment is often not indicated. Criteria to initiate antiarrhythmic therapy include signs of persistent tachycardia (>140 bpm), hypotension (systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg), hypoperfusion (prolonged capillary refill time, weak pulses), "R on T wave" pattern ( a phenomenon that predisposes to ventricular fibrillation), or multifocal ventricular premature contractions. A bolus of 2% lidocaine (2-4 mg/kg, slowly IV) can be administered and repeated twice in a 30-min period if necessary; a continuous IV infusion (30-80 mcglkg/min) may be indicated to control a.iThythmias. Cardiac arrhythmias associated with GOV are often difficult to control. If the arrhythmia is poorly responsive to this therapy, procaina­ mide (6--10 mg/kg, IV over 15 min) should be given. Life-threatening arrhythmias may respond to 200/o magnesiwn sulfate (0.15--0.3 mEq/kg, or 12.5--35 mg/kg, IV over 15--60 min). Less common postoperative complica­ tions can include life-threatening conditions such as sepsis, peritonitis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Overall mortality rate associated with GOV is -25o/o-30%. Risk factors associated with short-tenn death from GOV include duration of clinical signs >6 hr before exan1ination, perfom1ing splenectomy and a partial gastrectomy, hypotension at any time during hospitalization, peritonitis, sepsis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Preoperative plasma lactate concentration has been shown to be a good predictor of gastric necrosis and a negative prognostic indicator for outcome for dogs with GOV. Prophylactic gastropexy is CWTently being recommended by many veterinary surgeons for breeds at risk or for dogs with relatives that have been affected by GOV. Prophylactic gastropexy can be performed at fue time of sterilization surgeries (spay/neuter). Minimally invasive tectuuques such as laparoscopic-assisted gastropexy are gaining favor. Prophylactic gastropexy has not been shown to prevent development of GOV if petformed at the tin1e of neuter but has been shown to help prevent recurrence if perfom1ed at the time of the first GOV correction. However, in one study of five large dog breeds predisposed to GOV, mortality was reduced (versus no gastro­ pexy) ranging from 2.2:fold (Rottweiler) to 29.6-fold (Great Dane).
